⚡️Cognition just became heavy industry, and this article is the disclosure event. 

The dominant truth: water is the binding constraint of the AI buildout because it is the one input that cannot be arbitraged across geography, and everything else in the stack can. 

Capital moves at wire speed, chips ship, power gets built in eighteen months, but water is watershed-local, legally encumbered, and politically primal. The line in the piece that carries the whole thesis is the Nevada-Michigan sentence: a dry river in one basin cannot be offset by abundance in another. Every other constraint on AI is fungible. This one has coordinates.

RECs are claims that decouple the legal representation from the physical draw, fiat logic applied to electrons: buy a certificate in one geography, consume wet megawatts in another, report “water positive.” The 3x indirect multiple at Google and 20x at Meta means every published datacenter water number understates the true draw by an order of magnitude, which sets up a revision bomb: the coming political fight will be fought with numbers that suddenly get twenty times worse on restatement, and narrative risk of that shape never reprices gradually.

The mechanism nobody in the thread will name: the buildout’s speed is its water bill. The gas-heavy backbone got chosen because gas deploys fast, and thermoelectric generation is evaporative by design, wet cooling towers boiling rivers into the sky to make tokens. Behind-the-meter turbines, the current fashion for dodging interconnect queues, are the maximum-water path. Solar and wind consume almost nothing, but they lost the race on velocity. The industry selected the water-intensive route as the price of speed, which means the constraint tightens on the same schedule as the capex, not after it.

Water rights are the oldest continuously litigated property claims in America, prior appropriation doctrine, agricultural seniority, century-old compacts, and the claimants vote. Datacenter siting fights are already the hottest local politics in a dozen states. Now overlay the newest fact on the board: the federal government is taking equity in the AI complex. The sovereign shareholder acquires a direct financial interest in overriding local water objections, and the collision is fully predictable, federal preemption of water and land constraints for “strategic AI infrastructure” against the one resource where local claims are oldest and voters care most. The referee owns the team, and the next thing the team needs is the other team’s river.

Burry himself is detection-layer signal with unauthorized timing, per his entire career: the structural flaw he names is real and the pop he implies is not scheduled by it. And the constraint he is holding actually cuts against his trade in one decisive respect. Physical rationing does not deflate the sector, it concentrates it. Whoever locked water rights, interconnects, and cooling capacity early converts a commodity input into a moat, and scarcity becomes the incumbents’ pricing power. The bear case for aggregate capex fantasies and the bull case for resource-secured hyperscalers are the same fact. Rationing picks winners; it does not pick zero.

The asset implication closes the loop: water is the most underpriced scarce atom on earth, agriculture pays near zero for senior rights while the marginal industrial user now bidding is the most valuable industry in history. 

That spread closes. 

Water rights, basins with surplus, cooling-adjacent infrastructure, and the political jurisdictions that own wet geography move from externality to asset class inside this cycle.

Diffusion language models, which generate text by repeatedly filling in masked parts rather than writing strictly from left to right, are becoming a serious alternative to standard transformer language models, but the usual ways of improving reasoning after training were built for left-to-right generation and do not fit the diffusion models.

The authors of this paper introduce a self-training method in which the model first produces its own answer, then uses parts of that completed answer as helpful context while learning how earlier denoising steps should behave.

Instead of comparing teacher and student one next token at a time, it compares them at each denoising step, which matches how diffusion language models actually generate text. 

Across math and planning tasks, d-OPSD matches or beats supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning baselines, while needing far fewer optimization steps than the main RL baseline.
